title: Complex solutions of quadratics
keyIdea: When b² − 4ac is negative, a quadratic has no real roots, but it still has two complex roots. We extend the numbers with i, where i² = −1, so √(−n) = √n i: for example √(−16) = 4i. The quadratic formula then gives roots of the form p ± qi. For x² + 2x + 5 = 0, b² − 4ac = −16, so x = (−2 ± 4i) ÷ 2 = −1 ± 2i. When the coefficients are real, complex roots always come as a conjugate pair p + qi and p − qi, whose sum and product are real.
familyTip: Ask someone to pick a quadratic like x² + 4x + 13 = 0. Work out b² − 4ac together first. If it is negative, use i to finish, then check your answer by adding the two roots: you should get −b.

visual.caption: Work out b² − 4ac, then drag each equation to the kind of roots it has, or tap it and then a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: lift a parabola until its roots go complex, simplify √(−n), solve with the formula, drag conjugate roots, and read roots from a vertex.

kid: Some quadratics never cross the x-axis. Take x² + 4 = 0. That needs x² = −4. But any real number squared is zero or positive. So there is no real answer.
Mathematicians made a new number to fix this. It is called i, and i² = −1. Now √(−4) = √4 × √(−1) = 2i. So x² + 4 = 0 has two answers: x = 2i and x = −2i.

The quadratic formula still works. Find b² − 4ac first. If it is negative, its square root has an i in it. For x² + 2x + 5 = 0, b² − 4ac = 4 − 20 = −16, and √(−16) = 4i. So x = (−2 ± 4i) ÷ 2 = −1 ± 2i.

The two roots are a pair. One is p + qi and the other is p − qi. We call them conjugates. Add them and the i parts cancel. Multiply them and you get a real number too. That is why the equation has no i in it.
adult: Ages 16 to 18. Solving quadratics with complex roots opens the complex numbers unit of A-level Further Mathematics (AQA 7367, Edexcel 9FM0 Core Pure, OCR A H245). It also matches CCSS HSN-CN.C.7, which asks students to solve quadratics with real coefficients that have complex solutions. Notation follows those specifications. The imaginary unit is i with i² = −1. A complex number is written p + qi. For n > 0, √(−n) means the principal root √n i. The Argand diagram plots real parts across and imaginary parts up.

The lab has five tasks. Students drag y = x² + 2x + c up through two real roots, a repeated root and complex roots. On an Argand diagram, the two real roots meet and then split up and down as −1 ± qi. They simplify √(−9), √(−16) and √(−36), and see that multiplying by i turns a point through 90°. They solve two quadratics line by line, then drag a root so its conjugate follows and the quadratic stays real. Last, they read roots from the vertex form (x − p)² + k.

Common mistakes. Students often write √(−16) = −4, or put a ± inside the root as well as in the formula. They may say a negative discriminant means no solutions at all. Many divide only one part of −b ± √(b² − 4ac) by 2a. Others give a second root that is not the conjugate, such as −3 + 2i for 3 + 2i. Some confuse the vertex height k with the imaginary part √k.

practice.hint: Split it as √{=n*n} × √(−1), and use √(−1) = i.

practice.prompt: x² − {=2*p}x + {=p*p+q*q} = 0 has roots p ± qi. What is the real part p?
practice.hint: The real part of both roots is −b ÷ 2a.
practice.explain: −b ÷ 2a = {=2*p} ÷ 2 = {p}, so the roots have real part {p}.

practice.hint: b² − 4ac = 4 − 20. Take its square root with i, then divide everything by 2.
practice.explain: b² − 4ac = −16 and √(−16) = 4i, so x = (−2 ± 4i) ÷ 2 = −1 ± 2i. There are no real solutions, but there are two complex ones.

practice.prompt: x² + {=2*p}x + {=p*p+q*q} = 0 has roots −{p} ± qi. Find q.
practice.hint: Work out b² − 4ac, take its square root using i, then divide by 2a = 2.
practice.explain: b² − 4ac = {=4*p*p} − {=4*(p*p+q*q)} = −{=4*q*q}. Its square root is {=2*q}i, and {=2*q}i ÷ 2 = {q}i, so q = {q}.

practice.prompt: One root of a quadratic with real coefficients is 3 + 2i. What is the other root?
practice.hint: Complex roots of a real quadratic come as conjugates.
practice.explain: The conjugate of 3 + 2i is 3 − 2i: same real part, opposite imaginary part. Then the sum 6 and product 13 are real.

pool.hint: Split it as √25 × √(−1), then use √(−1) = i.

pool.prompt: The roots of x² + bx + c = 0 are {p} ± {q}i. What is c?
pool.hint: c is the product of the roots: (p + qi)(p − qi) = p² + q².
pool.explain: (p + qi)(p − qi) = p² + q² = {=p*p} + {=q*q} = {=p*p+q*q}, so c = {=p*p+q*q}.

pool.prompt: The roots of x² + bx + c = 0 are {p} ± {q}i. What is the sum of the roots?
pool.hint: Add them: the i parts cancel.
pool.explain: ({p} + {q}i) + ({p} − {q}i) = {=2*p}. The sum is real, and it equals −b.

pool.prompt: b² − 4ac = −20 for a quadratic with real coefficients. What are its roots like?
pool.hint: A negative discriminant means the curve never meets the x-axis.
pool.explain: There are no real roots, but the formula gives two complex roots p ± qi, a conjugate pair.

pool.hint: b² − 4ac = 16 − 52. Remember −b = +4, and divide both parts by 2.
i is defined by what its square is.
pool.explain: i is defined so that i² = −1. That is what lets √(−n) = √n i.

pool.prompt: y = (x − 3)² + 9 never meets the x-axis. What are the roots of (x − 3)² + 9 = 0?
pool.hint: Rearrange to (x − 3)² = −9, then take square roots with i.
pool.explain: (x − 3)² = −9, so x − 3 = ±3i and x = 3 ± 3i. The vertex height 9 gives √9 = 3, not 9.

pool.prompt: Sam solves x² + 6x + 10 = 0 and writes x = −6 ± 2i ÷ 2. What is the slip?
choices: Both −6 and 2i must be divided by 2: x = −3 ± i
pool.hint: The whole top line, −b ± √(b² − 4ac), is divided by 2a.
pool.explain: (−6 ± 2i) ÷ 2 = −3 ± i. Dividing only the i part by 2 is a common slip.

pool.hint: Sum of roots = −b and product = c.
pool.explain: Sum = 2 so b = −2. Product = 1² + 1² = 2 so c = 2. That gives x² − 2x + 2 = 0.
